title: A ring-buffer event logger: overwrite the oldest

prereqs.why: This is the structure itself: an array, two indices, and a modulo that turns it into a circle.
The slots are a vector sized once in the constructor and then only ever written through, never grown.
Three files are compiled separately and linked, so a signature that does not match its declaration is a link error rather than a compile error.
Every index here is taken modulo the capacity, and the one that is not is the bug that reads past the end.

statement:
**Milestone 2 of 3.** The logger now has to survive a flood: when the buffer
is full, the oldest event makes way for the newest.

### What is carried forward

Your `ring_buffer.cpp` from milestone 1 arrives here exactly as you left it,
and so does `ring_buffer.hpp` **if you changed it** — a file you never
touched has nothing of yours to carry, so you get this milestone's version
of it instead. Nothing you wrote is ever overwritten.

Either way, **it does not build yet**, and that is the milestone. The new
`main.cpp` calls three functions that have no definition:

```cpp
void set_overwrite(bool on);     // turn it on or off
bool overwriting() const;        // whether it is on
std::size_t dropped() const;     // how many have been dropped, ever
```

If your header came forward with you it does not declare them either, so add
the declarations as well. The first error you see tells you which of the two
you are in: `undefined symbol` is the linker asking for the definitions, and
`no member named 'set_overwrite'` is the compiler asking for the declaration.

(If you have not done milestone 1, the files here are a working milestone-1
answer, so you are not blocked.)

### The commands

The first line is the capacity. Every line after it is one command.

```
push <at> <text>   add an event; <at> is a whole number, <text> is one word
pop                remove and print the oldest event, or print `empty`
size               print `<held>/<capacity>`
dump               print every event held, oldest arrival first, or `(none)`
```

`push` prints nothing when it works. A command that is not one of these is
ignored, and so is a malformed one.

Two more commands:

```
overwrite on|off   turn overwriting on or off
dropped            print how many events have been dropped
```

### What it has to do

- A buffer starts with overwriting **off**, and then behaves exactly as it did
  in milestone 1. Every milestone-1 case runs again here.
- With overwriting **on**, a `push` into a full buffer drops the oldest event,
  counts it, stores the new one and succeeds. Nothing is printed.
- `dropped` counts events thrown away to make room, over the life of the
  buffer. **A `pop` is not a drop.**
- Turning overwriting off again restores the refusing behaviour, and does not
  reset the count.

### The sample

```
2
overwrite on
push 1 a
push 2 b
push 3 c              a is dropped
dump            ->    2 b
                      3 c
dropped         ->    1
overwrite off
push 4 d        ->    full
size            ->    2/2
```

### How it is checked

The cases are this milestone's **and** milestone 1's. A change that breaks
what already worked fails here, which is what makes this a project rather
than three exercises.
hints: Start with the compiler. It is telling you about three functions that are declared and not defined — that is a link error, not a syntax one, and it names them. Define them, even as one-liners, and the build goes green before any behaviour is right.

Dropping the oldest to make room is a pop you do not hand back: move `start_` on by one, take one off the count, and add one to the drop count. Then the ordinary push path puts the new event exactly where the dropped one was.

Two things are easy to get wrong here and both have a case. `dropped()` counts only events thrown away to make room, so `pop` must not touch it. And turning overwriting off has to put the milestone-1 behaviour back exactly — a full buffer refuses again, and the count so far is not reset.
